outcome: A May 2026 preprint by Suchanda Roy and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian gives a complete forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization of word-representability for near-triangulations (planar graphs in which every bounded face is a triangle), settling a substantial subclass of planar graphs while leaving the general planar-graph characterization open.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Characterise (non-)word-representable planar graphs' is stated as the general problem of deciding word-representability for arbitrary planar graphs. As of January 2024, only partial results were known: triangle-free planar graphs are word-representable, and K4-free near-triangulations are word-representable iff 3-colourable. In May 2026, Roy and Hariharasubramanian (arXiv:2605.25733, 'Characterization of Word-Representable Near-Triangulations') obtained a complete forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization of word-representability for the entire class of near-triangulations — including those containing K4, which the Wikipedia article explicitly flags as a previously open sub-question ('a characterisation is known for K4-free planar graphs' but not for K4-containing near-triangulations). The paper states it 'unifies previous findings across multiple subclasses—including polyomino triangulations, K4-free near-triangulations, and chordal near-triangulations—while also correcting errors in earlier research.' This is a genuine restriction of the stated problem (near-triangulations are a proper subclass of planar graphs, not a different problem), so under §3.1 it counts as a case settled, classified `partial`, direction `confirmed` (the characterization proves what was sought — a full description of the word-representable members — rather than refuting an expectation). The general planar-graph problem, and other planar subclasses beyond near-triangulations, remain open. I read the full PDF (via WebFetch) and found no mention of AI, machine learning, automated theorem provers, or SAT/computer search in the proof method or any acknowledgements section; the paper reads as traditional combinatorial/graph-theoretic argument (forbidden induced subgraphs via case analysis on triangulation structure). No retraction or dispute found; this appears to be a single, recent, undigested-by-experts preprint (no journal acceptance or expert digestion found), which is why it is classified `partial` rather than `resolved` for that piece — though note `partial` per the schema does not itself distinguish digestion status the way `resolved`/`claimed` do for full resolutions; I am treating 'digested' as not required for a `partial` case-result the way it is for a full `resolved`, since the schema's resolved/claimed distinction is specifically about full resolutions of the stated problem. The earlier arXiv:2508.15177 ('On the word-representability of Km-Kn graphs') found by triage studies a different graph family (complete multipartite-type graphs) and is not planar-specific, so it does not bear on this bullet — I did not rely on it.
competing_reading: One could argue near-triangulations, while formally a subclass of planar graphs, are close enough to being 'the interesting case' (triangle-rich planar graphs) that this is effectively most of the way to resolving the general problem — but the paper itself does not claim to settle general planar graphs, and non-near-triangulation planar graphs (e.g. those with larger non-triangular bounded faces) are untouched, so `partial` rather than `resolved` or a stronger characterization is the correct read. A stricter reading could also argue this is 'progress' rather than 'partial' since it's a preprint without expert digestion, but the schema's `partial` label is about scope (a case settled) rather than digestion status, which is orthogonal here since the case itself is fully and rigorously characterized (forbidden induced subgraphs), just not yet externally verified by other experts.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (survey citation, journal acceptance, or independent verification) of arXiv:2605.25733 would move this specific case toward being treated as solid; a further paper extending the characterization to all planar graphs (not just near-triangulations) would resolve the Wikipedia bullet itself.

judgement.doubts: Near-triangulations are a proper subclass of planar graphs, so this is a case, not the whole bullet. The preprint has not been reviewed; the paper says it corrects errors in earlier work, so a later reader should watch for responses. The Pith Review page was never opened and does not count as verification either way.
